name: forest south edge: trunk band under the canopy (cherry blossom)
label: jp_city/jp-forest-sk-band-M-0
reasons: 화풍: 칸 정보량이 기준보다 훨씬 낮음 (4/4)

surfaces.part: cherry blossom canopy (pink mass at top)
trunk band (brown trunk on dark green shadow)
pink petals and ground strip at bottom

answer.evidence: The silhouette is 16 px wide for rows 0-10, narrows at row 11, and is full width again for rows 12-14. Columns x=4, 8 and 11 show pink canopy at rows 0-4 or 0-5. Below that comes a vertical trunk and dark green shadow (rows 5-14), then pink petals at rows 13-15. Nothing in the canopy reads as a horizontal top surface. It has no front-edge line followed by eave shadow, no ellipse, and no visible contents. The canopy and trunk are both drawn face-on as vertical elevation, so the object reads as a front elevation.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a single 16x16 tile (a trunk band) with only 12 distinct colours. The references have a median of about 108 colours per tile and 427-567 colours overall, so it is roughly 9x lower on per-tile density. Flat-fill coverage is 0% and the dark edge pixels are 0% neutral, so the outline is tinted (dark brown/maroon beside the trunk), which matches Beodeul. The trunk itself shows only about 3 lightness steps (dark, mid, a pinkish highlight) against 5-6 in the references, with little per-bark grain or root flare shading. At this size it reads as a small, simple dark patch beside the richly shaded reference trunks. A single tile of a thin trunk band could excuse some sparseness, but 12 colours against about 108 is still far below the reference, and the shading ramp is shallow.

surfaces.part: cherry blossom canopy (pink foliage mass above trunk)
trunk band (brown trunk with dark green shadow)

answer.evidence: The tile is a front-on slice of a forest edge: pink blossom canopy in rows 0-4, then a brown trunk with dark green shade in rows 5-14 and pink petals and grass at the base in rows 13-15. The silhouette is a near-full 16px-wide rectangle (rows 0-10 at width 16, a slight narrowing at row 11, and 16 again to row 14). There is no ellipse, no front-edge line followed by an eave shadow, and no visible horizontal surface. Everything is a vertical face with foliage texture, so it reads as a front elevation rather than a three-quarter view.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a tiny trunk-band tile of about one 16x16 tile. It has 12 distinct colours in total, against 427 and 567 for the references, and a median of 12 colours per tile against about 108. That is roughly 9x lower, and as a single tile it is not a thin or sparse object, so the density fact counts against it. By eye it shows a dark trunk with a pinkish canopy fringe and only about 3 distinct lightness steps on the trunk, where the references use 5-6 on bark and foliage. Flat-fill coverage is 0% and the dark edge pixels are 0% neutral, so the outlines are tinted dark tones rather than black stickers. The surface has a little variation but no per-clump or per-bark-ridge shading of the kind the references show. It is cleanly built but clearly shallower and less textured than the Beodeul trees, so it does not meet the bar.

surfaces.part: cherry blossom canopy (pink foliage mass at top)

answer.evidence: The tile is a band of tree trunk seen face-on under a pink canopy. Columns x=8 and x=11 show the trunk as a single vertical run (rows 4/5 to 14) with no front-edge line, eave shadow, or ellipse. The width profile is nearly constant at 16 for rows 0-14, so there is no widening and narrowing. The pink foliage at the top is a front-facing mass, not a horizontal surface. The trunk is therefore only a vertical face, with no distinguishable top plane.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a tiny single-tile trunk band, so I judged it by eye as well as by the numbers. It has only 12 distinct colours in total and a tile median of 12, against about 108 per tile and 427-567 colours in the references. That is far below both. Flat-fill coverage is 0%, so there are no large flat areas, and the dark edge pixels are 0% neutral, so the outline is tinted and not a sticker line. Even so, the trunk and bark show only about 3 lightness steps, where the references use 5-6 on bark and canopy. The bark grain is minimal and there are no clumped highlights or root detail like the references' trunks. The pink/dark tones are muddy and clustered, with little ramp structure. A careful artist would find this noticeably thinner and flatter than the Beodeul trees, so it fails.

surfaces.part: trunk (brown, dark green shadow between roots)
fallen petals and ground at the base

answer.evidence: The tile is a face-on strip. Pink canopy fills rows 0-4 across the full 16px width, then the trunk runs down rows 5-14 with dark green shadow on both sides and petals at rows 13-15. The width profile is 16 for rows 0-10, narrows to 12 at row 11, returns to 16, then drops to 10 at row 15. It has no ellipse, no front-edge line followed by eave shadow, and no sloped plane. The canopy is a flat vertical mass, not a visible horizontal top. Only the front face is shown, so it matches the front-elevation reference examples.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a single 16x16 tile, a trunk band with a bit of canopy, and it is tiny next to the full reference trees. Its measured facts are far below both references: 12 distinct colours in total against 427 and 567, and a median of 12 per tile against about 108. Flat-fill coverage is 0%, and the dark edge pixels carry a tint (0% neutral), so the outline reads as dark material tone rather than near-black. By eye, the trunk and the dark foliage look like only about 3 lightness steps, with a few speckles of pink and green. The references have 5-6 steps per material, with clumped leaf highlights and shaded roots. A trunk band can legitimately be sparse, but 12 colours in a full tile is much thinner than the reference tile density, and the shading is shallow. A careful artist would not accept it next to the references without it looking flatter.
